title: Chapter 9 — The Sermon
paragraphs: Father Mapple rose, and in a mild voice of unassuming authority ordered the scattered people to close up. "Starboard gangway, there! Side away to port — port gangway to starboard! Midships! Midships!"
There was a low rumbling of heavy sea boots among the benches and an even slighter shuffling of women's shoes, and then all was quiet again, every eye on the preacher.

He paused a moment, then kneeled in the bow of the pulpit, folded his large brown hands across his chest, raised his closed eyes, and offered a prayer so deeply reverent that he seemed to be kneeling and praying at the bottom of the sea.

When he finished, in prolonged, solemn tones — like the continuous tolling of a bell on a ship foundering at sea in fog — he began reading the following hymn. But as he reached the final stanzas, his manner changed, and he burst forth with pealing joy and exultation:
"The ribs and terrors in the whale / Arched over me a dismal gloom, / While all God's sunlit waves rolled by, / And lifted me deepening down to doom.
"I saw the opening jaws of hell, / With endless pains and sorrows there; / Which none but those who feel can tell — / Oh, I was plunging to despair.
"In black distress, I called my God, / When I could hardly think him mine; / He bent his ear to my complaints — / No more the whale did me confine.
"Swiftly he flew to my relief, / As though on a shining dolphin borne; / Fearsome, yet bright, as lightning shone / The face of my Deliverer God.
"My song forever shall record / That terrible, that joyful hour; / I give the glory to my God, / His all the mercy and the power."

Nearly everyone joined in singing this hymn, which swelled high above the howling of the storm. A brief pause followed; the preacher slowly turned over the pages of the Bible, and at last, laying his hand flat on the proper page, said: "Beloved shipmates, clinch the last verse of the first chapter of Jonah — 'And God had prepared a great fish to swallow up Jonah.'"

"Shipmates, this book, containing only four chapters — four yarns — is one of the smallest strands in the mighty cable of the Scriptures. Yet what depths of the soul Jonah's deep sea-line sounds! What a pregnant lesson this prophet is to us! What a noble thing is that canticle in the fish's belly! How billow-like and boisterously grand! We feel the floods surging over us; we sound with him to the kelpy bottom of the waters; seaweed and all the slime of the sea is around us! But what is this lesson that the book of Jonah teaches? Shipmates, it is a two-stranded lesson: a lesson to us all as sinful men, and a lesson to me as a pilot of the living God. As sinful men, it is a lesson to us all, because it is a story of the sin, the hard-heartedness, the suddenly awakened fears, the swift punishment, the repentance, the prayers, and finally the deliverance and joy of Jonah. As with all sinners among men, the sin of this son of Amittai lay in his willful disobedience of the command of God — never mind now what that command was, or how it was conveyed — which he found a hard command. But all the things that God would have us do are hard for us to do — remember that — and so he more often commands us than tries to persuade us. And if we obey God, we must disobey ourselves; and it is in this disobeying of ourselves that the hardness of obeying God consists.

"With this sin of disobedience in him, Jonah flouts God still further by trying to flee from Him. He thinks that a ship made by men will carry him into countries where God does not reign, but only the Captains of this earth. He skulks about the wharves of Joppa, and looks for a ship that's bound for Tarshish. Perhaps there lurks a meaning here that no one has noticed until now. By all accounts Tarshish could have been no other city than the modern Cadiz. That's the opinion of learned men. And where is Cadiz, shipmates? Cadiz is in Spain; as far by water from Joppa as Jonah could possibly have sailed in those ancient days, when the Atlantic was an almost unknown sea. Because Joppa, the modern Jaffa, shipmates, is on the most easterly coast of the Mediterranean, the Syrian coast; and Tarshish, or Cadiz, is more than two thousand miles to the west of that, just outside the Straits of Gibraltar. Don't you see, then, shipmates, that Jonah sought to flee the whole width of the world from God? Miserable man! Oh! Most contemptible and worthy of all scorn; with slouched hat and guilty eye, skulking from his God; prowling among the shipping like a vile burglar hurrying to cross the seas. His look is so disordered and self-condemning that if there had been policemen in those days, Jonah would have been arrested on the mere suspicion of something wrong before he touched a deck. How plainly he's a fugitive! No baggage, not a hat-box, valise, or carpetbag — no friends come with him to the wharf to say goodbye. At last, after much dodging search, he finds the Tarshish ship taking on the last items of her cargo; and as he steps on board to see its Captain in the cabin, all the sailors stop hoisting in the goods for the moment, to take note of the stranger's evil eye. Jonah sees this; but in vain he tries to look all ease and confidence; in vain he attempts his wretched smile. The sailors' strong intuitions about the man assure them he can be no innocent. In their playful but still serious way, one whispers to another — 'Jack, he's robbed a widow'; or, 'Joe, do you see him? He's a bigamist'; or, 'Harry lad, I guess he's the adulterer that broke jail in old Gomorrah, or maybe one of the missing murderers from Sodom.' Another runs to read the notice that's stuck up against the post on the wharf where the ship is moored, offering five hundred gold coins for the capture of a parricide, and giving a description of his person. He reads, and looks from Jonah to the notice; while all his sympathetic shipmates now crowd around Jonah, ready to lay their hands on him. Frightened Jonah trembles, and summoning all his boldness into his face, only looks all the more a coward. He will not admit that he is suspected; but that in itself is strong grounds for suspicion. So he makes the best of it; and when the sailors find that he is not the man in the notice, they let him pass, and he goes down into the cabin.

"'Who's there?' cries the Captain at his busy desk, hurriedly making out his papers for the Customs — 'Who's there?' Oh! How that harmless question mangles Jonah! For an instant he almost turns to flee again. But he rallies. 'I want a passage in this ship to Tarshish; how soon do you sail, sir?' So far the busy Captain had not looked up at Jonah, though the man now stands in front of him; but no sooner does he hear that hollow voice than he darts a searching glance at him. 'We sail with the next tide,' he answered at last, slowly, still eyeing him intently. 'No sooner, sir?' — 'Soon enough for any honest man who goes as a passenger.' Ha! Jonah, that's another stab. But he swiftly calls the Captain away from that scent. 'I'll sail with you,' he says — 'the passage money, how much is that? I'll pay now.' For it is particularly written, shipmates, as if it were a thing not to be overlooked in this history, 'that he paid the fare thereof' before the ship sailed. And taken with the context, this is full of meaning.

"Now Jonah's Captain, shipmates, was one whose discernment detects crime in anyone, but whose greed exposes it only in the penniless. In this world, shipmates, sin that pays its way can travel freely, and without a passport; whereas Virtue, if a pauper, is stopped at every frontier. So Jonah's Captain gets ready to test the length of Jonah's purse before he judges him openly. He charges him three times the usual sum; and Jonah agrees to it. Then the Captain knows that Jonah is a fugitive; but at the same time he resolves to help a flight that paves its trail with gold. Yet when Jonah actually takes out his purse, prudent suspicions still trouble the Captain. He rings every coin to find a counterfeit. 'Not a forger, anyway,' he mutters; and Jonah is entered for his passage. 'Show me my stateroom, sir,' says Jonah now; 'I'm travel-weary; I need sleep.' 'You look it,' says the Captain; 'there's your room.' Jonah goes in, and would lock the door, but the lock has no key. Hearing him foolishly fumbling there, the Captain laughs quietly to himself, and mutters something about how the doors of convicts' cells are never allowed to be locked from inside. All dressed and dusty as he is, Jonah throws himself into his berth, and finds the little stateroom's ceiling almost resting on his forehead. The air is close, and Jonah gasps. Then, in that cramped hole, sunk too beneath the ship's waterline, Jonah feels a foreboding, like a herald, of that stifling hour when the whale will hold him in the smallest of the prison wards of his bowels.

"Screwed at its axis against the side, a swinging lamp gently oscillates in Jonah's room; and as the ship heels over toward the wharf with the weight of the last bales taken on, the lamp, flame and all, though slightly moving, still keeps a permanent slant in relation to the room; though in truth, being itself unfailingly straight, it only makes obvious the false, lying levels among which it hangs. The lamp alarms and frightens Jonah; as he lies in his berth his tormented eyes roll around the place, and this so far successful fugitive finds no refuge for his restless glance. But that contradiction in the lamp appalls him more and more. The floor, the ceiling, and the side are all awry. 'Oh! So my conscience hangs in me!' he groans. 'Straight upward it burns; but the chambers of my soul are all in crookedness!'

"Like one who after a night of drunken revelry hurries to his bed, still reeling, but with his conscience still pricking him, just as the plunging of the Roman racehorse only strikes the steel tags hung on it all the deeper into its flesh; like one who in that miserable plight still turns and turns in giddy anguish, praying God for annihilation until the fit has passed; and at last, amid the whirl of woe he feels, a deep stupor steals over him, as over a man who bleeds to death, for conscience is the wound, and there is nothing to stanch it; so, after sore wrestlings in his berth, Jonah's prodigy of ponderous misery drags him drowning down to sleep.

"And now the time of the tide has come; the ship casts off her cables; and from the deserted wharf the uncheered ship for Tarshish, heeling far over, glides out to sea. That ship, my friends, was the first smuggler on record! The contraband was Jonah. But the sea rebels; it will not bear the wicked burden. A dreadful storm comes on; the ship is about to break up. But now, when the boatswain calls all hands to lighten her; when boxes, bales, and jars are clattering overboard; when the wind is shrieking, and the men are yelling, and every plank thunders with trampling feet right over Jonah's head; in all this raging tumult, Jonah sleeps his hideous sleep. He sees no black sky and raging sea, does not feel the reeling timbers, and little does he hear or heed the distant rush of the mighty whale, which even now, with open mouth, is cleaving the seas after him. Yes, shipmates, Jonah had gone down into the sides of the ship — a berth in the cabin, as I take it — and was fast asleep. But the frightened master comes to him, and shrieks in his dead ear, 'What do you mean, O sleeper? Arise!' Startled from his lethargy by that dreadful cry, Jonah staggers to his feet, and stumbling up to the deck, grasps a shroud, one of the ropes bracing the mast, to look out at the sea. But at that moment a panther of a billow leaps over the bulwarks and springs on him. Wave after wave leaps into the ship like this, and finding no quick way out, runs roaring fore and aft, until the sailors come close to drowning while still afloat. And every time the white moon shows her frightened face from the steep gullies in the blackness overhead, aghast Jonah sees the rearing bowsprit pointing high upward, but soon beaten downward again toward the tormented deep.

"Terrors upon terrors run shouting through his soul. In all his cringing postures, the God-fugitive is now too plainly recognized. The sailors take note of him; their suspicions of him grow more and more certain, and at last, to test the truth fully by referring the whole matter to high Heaven, they fall to casting lots, to see on whose account this great tempest has come upon them. The lot is Jonah's; and once that is discovered, how furiously they mob him with their questions. 'What is your occupation? Where do you come from? Your country? What people?' But note now, my shipmates, the behavior of poor Jonah. The eager sailors only ask him who he is, and where he is from; yet they receive not only an answer to those questions, but also an answer to a question they did not put; and that unasked answer is forced from Jonah by the hard hand of God that is upon him.

"'I am a Hebrew,' he cries — and then — 'I fear the Lord, the God of Heaven, who has made the sea and the dry land!' Fear Him, O Jonah? Yes, well might you fear the Lord God then! Right away he goes on to make a full confession; at which the sailors become more and more appalled, but still they pity him. For when Jonah, not yet begging God for mercy, since he knew all too well the darkness of what he deserved — when wretched Jonah cries out to them to take him and throw him into the sea, for he knew that it was for his sake this great tempest was upon them, they mercifully turn from him, and look for other ways to save the ship. But all in vain; the indignant gale howls louder; then, with one hand raised to God in prayer, with the other they, not without reluctance, lay hold of Jonah.

"And now see Jonah lifted up like an anchor and dropped into the sea; and at once an oily calm drifts in from the east, and the sea goes still, as Jonah takes the gale down with him and leaves smooth water behind. He sinks into the whirling heart of such a masterless turmoil that he barely notices the moment he drops, seething, into the gaping jaws that wait for him; and the whale slams all his ivory teeth shut on his prison, like so many white bolts. Then Jonah prayed to the Lord from the belly of the fish. But look at his prayer, and learn a weighty lesson. For sinful as he is, Jonah doesn't weep and wail to be rescued outright. He feels that his terrible punishment is just. He leaves his rescue entirely to God, and is content with this: that despite all his pains and pangs, he will still look toward His holy temple. And here, shipmates, is true and faithful repentance; not loudly demanding pardon, but grateful for punishment. And how much this conduct of Jonah's pleased God is shown when He finally delivers him from the sea and the whale. Shipmates, I don't set Jonah before you to be imitated in his sin; but I do set him before you as a model of repentance. Don't sin; but if you do, make sure you repent of it the way Jonah did."

While he spoke these words, the howling of the shrieking, slanting storm outside seemed to add new power to the preacher. Describing Jonah's storm, he seemed tossed by a storm himself. His deep chest heaved like a ground swell; his tossed arms seemed the warring elements at work; and the thunder rolling from his dark brow and the light leaping from his eyes made every simple listener watch him with a strange, quick fear.
Then a lull came over his expression as he silently turned the pages of the Book once more. At last, standing motionless with closed eyes, he seemed for a moment to be communing with God and himself.
But again he leaned toward the congregation, and bowing his head low, with an expression of the deepest yet manliest humility, he spoke these words:

"Shipmates, God has laid just one hand on you; both his hands press down on me. By whatever murky light I have, I have read you the lesson that Jonah teaches all sinners; and so to you, and still more to me, because I am a greater sinner than you. And now how gladly I would come down from this masthead and sit on the hatches there where you are sitting, and listen as you listen, while one of you read me that other and more awful lesson — the one Jonah teaches me, as a pilot of the living God. How Jonah — an anointed pilot-prophet, or speaker of true things, commanded by the Lord to sound those unwelcome truths in the ears of wicked Nineveh — appalled at the hostility he would stir up, fled from his mission, and tried to escape his duty and his God by taking ship at Joppa. But God is everywhere; Jonah never reached Tarshish. As we have seen, God came down on him in the whale and swallowed him into living gulfs of doom, and with swift, slanting plunges dragged him 'into the midst of the seas,' where the swirling depths sucked him ten thousand fathoms down, and 'the weeds were wrapped about his head,' and the whole watery world of woe rolled over him. Yet even then, beyond the reach of any plumb line — 'out of the belly of hell' — when the whale ran aground on the ocean's deepest bones, even then God heard the swallowed, repenting prophet when he cried out. Then God spoke to the fish; and up from the shuddering cold and blackness of the sea the whale came breaching toward the warm and pleasant sun and all the delights of air and earth, and 'vomited out Jonah upon the dry land'; and the word of the Lord came a second time; and Jonah, bruised and beaten — his ears, like two seashells, still murmuring with the ocean's countless voices — Jonah did what the Almighty told him. And what was that, shipmates? To preach the Truth to the face of Falsehood! That was it!

"This, shipmates, this is that other lesson; and woe to the pilot of the living God who takes it lightly. Woe to the man whom this world lures away from his Gospel duty! Woe to the man who tries to pour oil on the waters when God has brewed them into a gale! Woe to the man who tries to please rather than to appall! Woe to the man whose good name matters more to him than goodness! Woe to the man who, in this world, does not court dishonor! Woe to the man who would not be true, even if being false meant salvation! Yes, woe to the man who, as the great Pilot Paul says, preaches to others and is himself a castaway!"

He dropped and fell away from himself for a moment; then, lifting his face to them again, he showed a deep joy in his eyes, as he cried out with a heavenly enthusiasm: "But oh! Shipmates! On the starboard hand of every woe there is a sure delight; and the top of that delight is higher than the bottom of the woe is deep. Is not the main-truck at the masthead higher than the kelson is low? Delight is to him — a far, far upward and inward delight — who against the proud gods and commodores of this earth always stands forth as his own inexorable self. Delight is to him whose strong arms still hold him up when the ship of this base, treacherous world has gone down beneath him. Delight is to him who gives no quarter in the truth, and kills, burns, and destroys all sin, though he pluck it out from under the robes of Senators and Judges. Delight — top-gallant delight is to him who acknowledges no law or lord but the Lord his God, and is only a patriot to heaven. Delight is to him whom all the waves of the billows of the seas of the boisterous mob can never shake from this sure Keel of the Ages. And eternal delight and deliciousness will be his who, coming to lay himself down, can say with his final breath — O Father! — known to me chiefly by Your rod — mortal or immortal, here I die. I have striven to be Yours, more than to be this world's, or my own. Yet this is nothing: I leave eternity to You; for what is man that he should live out the lifetime of his God?"
He said no more. Slowly waving a benediction, he covered his face with his hands and remained kneeling until every person had left and he was alone in the place.
